newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks green vote, Dole hits Hollywood.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks green vote, Dole hits Hollywood.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton bid for the "green vote" on Wednesday while Bob Dole hit Hollywood for glorifying drugs as a new Reuters poll showed Clinton far ahead in crucial Midwest states.

The Reuters/Zogby poll of likely voters in Ohio, Michigan and Illinois found Clinton ahead of Dole 47.3 percent to 32.2 percent in the overall three-state sampling. Ross Perot polled 4.4 percent and 15 percent were undecided.

Clinton's lead was widest in Michigan, where he was more than 20 points ahead of Dole, 50 percent to 29.5 percent. In Illinois, the president's advantage was about 16 points, 48.2 percent to 32.4 percent. The race was closest in Ohio, where Clinton led by 13 points, 45.7 to 32.3 percent.
The poll, which surveyed 1,325 likely voters, had a margin of error of five percentage points for each individual state and three points overall.

The three states carry 61 votes in the Electoral College, 22 percent of the 270 needed to be elected president. Many analysts believe Dole probably needs to carry two of the three to win the Nov. 5 election.

A Gallup tracking poll showed Clinton's lead over Dole nationally was back to 17 percentage points, from 14 points on Tuesday. He led Dole 52 percent to 35 percent, with Perot trailing with five percent.

An NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll of 1,623 registered voters conducted Sept. 12-17 gave the Clinton-Gore ticket a 51 percent to 38 percent lead over the Dole-Kemp ticket. The Perot-Choate ticket was favoured by five percent in the poll, which has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 points.

Clinton used the majestic panorama of the Grand Canyon to announce a plan to protect vast stretches of red rock canyons and plateaus in Utah from development. The decision was hailed by environmentalists but denounced by those who want to develop the territory for coal mining.
While mining was important to the nation's economy, Clinton said, "We can't have mines everywhere and we shouldn't have mines that threaten our national treasures."
Calling the area "some of the most remarkable land in the world," Clinton said "in protecting it we live up to our obligation to preserve a national heritage."
Polls indicate the environment is an important issue for a sizeable group of voters, who heavily favour Clinton.
Dole was in Los Angeles, where he criticised the entertainment industry for glorifying drug use and unveiled a new anti-drug slogan -- "Just don't do it."

"I have a message to the fashion, music and film industries," he said. "Take your influence seriously, you have a lot of it. Respect your talent and power. Stop the commercialization of drug abuse. Stop the glorification of slow suicide."

The speech was the latest salvo in Dole's effort to win votes with an anti-drugs, anti-crime programme. The entertainment and fashion industries shared responsibility for shaping attitudes among teenagers, whose rates of drug use have more than doubled since 1992, Dole said.

Texas billionaire Ross Perot, in his first appearance since the commission on presidential debates recommended his exclusion from the upcoming presidential debates, told a San Francisco audience the voters were being deprived of the opportunity to hear his views.

"Any candidate who is excluded from these debates cannot present his views to the 80 million voters under any other method," he said. He also complained the national television networks were refusing to sell him advertising time for his 30-minute "infommercials."

The Dole and Clinton campaigns held no negotiations about the debates on Wednesday and blamed each other for the delay. It was becoming increasingly clear they would not meet the schedule originally proposed by the commission, under which the first debate was to take place next Wednesday.

In Washington, a Republican congressional report charged that Clinton had abused his power and obstructed investigations into 1993 White House travel office firings. The House Government Reform and Oversight Committee issued 21 pages of excerpts from a more detailed report to be made public later.

In one of a series of findings on the so-called "Travelgate" affair, the report said: "President Clinton has engaged in an unprecedented misuse of the executive power, abuse of executive privilege and obstruction of numerous investigations into the travel office."

Before walking out on a vote to adopt the report, Democrats called it a "partisan smear" and a "multimillion dollar witchhunt" and Clinton's special associate counsel Mark Fabiani called it "an election-year stunt."
